o: Count circular windows of 3 consecutive tiles whose colors alternate (middle differs from both neighbors, forcing ends equal). For colors = [0,1,0,0,1], the windows starting at indices 0, 2, 4 are alternating, giving 3. With n ≤ 100 we can simply test all n starting positions using modular indexing — no fancy machinery needed.
k: A triple alternates iff c[i] != c[i+1] and c[i+1] != c[i+2].
Circularity is handled with indices mod n.

a.i: For each start i, verify the two adjacent-color inequalities on tiles i, i+1, i+2 (mod n). Every alternating triple is counted exactly once by its start.
s: Count i where colors[i] != colors[(i+1)%n] and colors[(i+1)%n] != colors[(i+2)%n].
a.t: O(n) — one constant-time test per starting tile

a.i: Concatenate the first two tiles onto the array so every circular window becomes a linear one, then slide a window of size 3 counting alternating patterns. Identical complexity, sometimes easier to reason about.
s: Count i where b[i] != b[i+1] and b[i+1] != b[i+2] for i in 0..n-1.
a.t: O(n) — linear scan of the doubled array

w: Either approach is fine at this scale; the modular-index version avoids extra memory. Pitfall: forgetting the wrap-around (checking only i ≤ n-3 misses groups spanning the seam) — examples like [1,1,1] → 0 and [0,1,0,0,1] → 3 cover it. Follow-up: this is the warm-up for Alternating Groups II (fixed window size k) and III (updates), where sliding-window and data-structure techniques take over.
